text:
Hardware Unboxed makes good, thorough reviews of products. It's important to ask questions such as "Is this new technology really worth it?" Just because Nvidia makes the best absolute performance product on the market, does not mean that it's a good purchase. Just because it's the best does not mean that they can just price it however they want. A good product is priced in accordance to its comparative performance, a great product is priced lower than products of similar performance. A product that is 5% better should not command a 30% higher price tag, for example.
Nvidia has always been about pushing new proprietary technologies out very early and using that to grab the market. So naturally they're not going to be pleased when someone comes out and says that their new technologies are mostly gimmicks.

text:
RTX 2060's "6GB vRAM" is a problem!

• At present, many games already use more than 6GB at 1080p ultra. Example: Final Fantasy XV, Shadow of War, Rise of The Tomb Raider, Shadow of The Tomb Raider(DX12), COD BO 4, COD WW II, Battlefield V (DX12), Resident Evil 7, Deus Ex MD... etc.

• Future games will require high vRAM.

• DX12 uses more vRAM than DX11. Future games will be DX12 resulting higher vRAM usage.

• Enabling DXR (Ray Tracing) increases vRAM consumption.

• Enabling DLSS doesn't make vRAM usage any lower.

• Even lower end cards like RX 580, 590, GTX 1070 non Ti has more vRAM than RTX 2060.

• Nvidia themselves told PCWorld that they could've outfitted the RTX 2060 with 8GB of GDDR6 but they made it 6GB to reduce cost. Though they expect games to utilize full 8GB of vRAM in a year or two.

Nvidia is trying to attract people with fancy RTX features which are half-baked and giving lower vRAM so that RTX 2060 owners will upgrade faster.
Also the point is 6GB won't be enough for RTX 2060.

text:
The fact that you give honest reviews is what keeps me subbed and watching.  If companies don't like your honesty, that's on them, and viewers/customers like me aren't going to give a spit about who has the first reviews.   I know I don't care a lick about who has the first reviews.  I care explicitly about who has the most valid and honest reviews, and I sub to several of the best tech review channels I've found for consistently great info on this stuff.  

Yours is one of those channels.  

In all my years of parsing through and leaning on channels like yours for good information, you've never steered me wrong, you've cheerfully owned mistakes when you've made them and you've never done anything that's made me think 'That guy is shilling for a brand' at all.   Stay honest and let nVidia show itself to be run by shortsighted, temperamental children if that's how they choose to behave.       I'll stop buying nVidia cards long before I could even imagine caring about who has reviews out first.

I know that 'first = best' is a common mentality for some, even in the purchasing of expensive PC hardware...but would I be out of line to suspect that most of us aren't stupid with our money even if we're fairly wealthy?       I can't help but suspect that racing to be the first to review something like a GPU isn't as compelling as nVidia probably hopes it is.

Because I know for certain that I'll wait for reviews from Gamers Nexus and yourself on such things before I'll even care what JayzTwoCents, Linus Tech Tips, Bitwit or UFD Tech have to say.    I like all of those channels for various reasons, but when I want no-bullshit information, I look for the Hardware Unboxed and Gamers Nexus reviews.

JayzTwoCents is fun to watch.  He's a very entertaining guy, but he makes no particular effort to be scientific and his personal favorites for things are obvious.   Linus is also a great entertainer and fun to watch, but often takes 15 minutes to say almost nothing at all, even if he said it very amusingly.    

Bitwit's channel is pretty decent, but again he and Jay have personal favorites for things that are obvious.  Again, nothing wrong with that for funsies and having a good ol' time...but not where I look for straight talk, no-favorites-played data on what performs, how and how well compared to the other stuff.

UFD Tech...again, much the same.  I enjoy UFD Tech for the conversation points he brings up that are contrary to my own.  He makes intelligent points on topics, particularly crypto markets, that I don't always agree with or even like, but they're intelligent and I can tell I'd very much enjoy discussing such things with him in person, hypothetically.   Lots of opinions, not so much hard data.

Gamer's Nexus roams without apology into the shallow edge of electrical engineer/whitesheet data points, and as an electrical engineer, I really like that.  I know what GN Steve is talking about at least as often as he does, and I very much enjoy the teardown and hardware-oriented reviews they do.

And I honestly can't think of a better channel than yours for getting straight to the point about what most gamers care about; the performance.     You talk about the market and current events, but you've got a great sense of how to say just enough without it being too little and seeming anemic or too much and dragging it on before you get to the charts and dissembling your findings.

You and Steve from GN are my go-to's for information that matters in the PC consumer hardware biz here on YouTube.     And while I have no good way of communicating to you how much of a finicky PITA hardass I am about data sources, know that you deserve some sort of award for that.

text:
See, this is why I & many others do and will continue to watch/read your content Steve. Bc you keep your integrity as opposed to "selling out" or becoming shills for one or both companies. And this will pay off in the long run. Like you said, you're working for us, on our side, not them or on theirs. And it is us that help keep you afloat and put food on the table. Sure, there's 2 sides to this equation, in that they are the ones that provide you the actual product to review. But without us, there would be no reason or purpose for any of your work whatsoever. You might as well try to sell forks to dogs. One of us can be "replaced" (them) while the other absolutely can't (us). 

You are a consumer advocate, not a member of their marketing arm. They don't directly pay you a salary in order to have you do exactly what Mr. Boss tells you to. Well neither do we, but like I said, it's bc of us you're doing what you do in the first place, not them. No us, no job. We are your end customers, your market (along with ad companies I'm sure. But same goes for them as well. No us, no readership/viewership, no ads), while they are not your employer. Keep doing what you do the way you have and we'll continue to support you so you can bypass them and continue to produce the great content & data that you have been. We can replace them and actually become both sides of the equation, supporting you both directly & indirectly. And keeping your integrity + providing honest, unbiased reviews will go a long way. More integrity means more respect from the community. More respect means more trust. More trust means overall more growth, more reach, more power, and your words having a greater impact and value as a whole. Making you an indispensable voice. Soon the tables might even actually turn and they become the ones trembling at your feet, afraid to get on your bad side, for fear of your influence. Trust me, you do not want to go too far in the opposite direction. Look at Tom's HW and where that has got them. Throwing their respect completely out the window and just being a laughing stock of a meme of a joke of a site. Their words & views are utterly meaningless to anyone besides fanboys and/or those who are serious about this industry/hobby. They hold absolutely no weight nor value. This is where shilling takes you. You start to suck up to these companies as a way get ahead or stay in the game, but in the end you start relying on them too much as to lose your independence. Becoming so dependent on them you essentially just end up being under their wing, w/ them basically owning you. Which I'm sure they'd love. Cheapest acquisition in history. Paid purely in early review sample video cards lol. And ppl will catch on sooner or later. Once that goes, the first thing to go w/ it is your reputation. Which is everything in journalism/the press.

Anyways just know you've got your supporters bc of exactly how you carry out your business. Keep your head up and don't change, it's all for the best in the long run. As an added bonus, you might actually sleep better at night too lol. It's a shame Nvidia don't think you're propaganda enough for them. But not really. More like an honor in my book.

text:
Something unusual, good, but unusual, has happened with this video.  A general trend here on YouTube is a decline in the percentage of "Likes" as the number of views increases.  What I've informally observed is that about 15% of viewers will "Like" a video when it is first released.  Perhaps this is due to a channel's regular viewers being more apt to show their approval.  Then, as folks who may not regularly watch a channel's videos, the ratio of "Views" to "Likes" will decrease down to 10% then 5%, more or less and generally speaking.

This video has definitely bucked that trend.  Fifteen hours after being uploaded, with over 81,000 views, the number of "Likes" is 9100.  It still has more than 10% of its viewers giving it a thumbs up.

If I were Nvidia, this is a telling fact of which I would take great heed.  Perhaps it means the they are losing control of the narrative.

@Hardwareunboxed  About Linus Media Group I think that's because they're less of a tech review thing now, and more of a "consumer" review thing. Like they may expand into cars, they already test general tech products like laptops and phones and way beyond computers like IoT, etc.

Now about this Nvidia fallout with you guys. First of all, THANK YOU SO MUCH for being a voice of reason and sticking to your guns. You might lose an unfair battle today (insofar as you can't do anything to get Nvidia to send you stuff...), but comfort yourselves in knowing that you are winning the long-term important mindshare battle of "who can I trust?" as reviewers, as media pundits -- I, for one, will never forget that you are one of the good guys, read: integrity (conforming your actions to your words) and honesty (conforming your words to your actions).

I'll add one thing. Day 1 reviews are probably important to your bottom line so I can't speak about that. What I can say is that products live a long time, years, and most of us don't buy day 1; we go back and scout the market months, years after to compare stuff and get good bang for the buck. How many 1080Ti reviews did I watch in Q3-Q4 2018 because it made sense. That's not "evergreen", but it's as close as it gets: a perfectly well done review, the likes of yours, Nexus, Anandtech. We go back to these, over and over again.

That's your gold. That's the value you add to the tech table. It'll pay off many times. Perhaps long after Nvidia as a company is dead (remember, half of the Fortune 500 doesn't exist 30 years later, and that's accelerating). I don't know of a short term solution, maybe some of you guys "small/medium" sized should partner up with others to become big enough to command more marketing oomph (so they can't ignore you), maybe create a press-alliance-federation of sorts where "we don't release shit until all members have access to the product" (that would certainly be a weapon against marketing choosing which reviewers to supply). Idk. But please keep at it, this is the good fight, and a fantastic job.

text:
You seem unhappy Steve. Well, Nvidia might have been salty because you didn't recommend their RTX 2080 card at launch, to which I would say
- It's within your rights and is an honest opinion. Heck, I agree with you on this point as well.
- It's within their rights to not partner with reviewers who cast a negative shadow on their products.

I think it's a dilemma for the Nvidia PR team right now. If they continue to provide you with their new GPU's, they surely get more coverage, but they fear that you will bash on the new products. If they don't, they may get more favourable reviews from other reviewers, but there's a chance that you might upload this video, which you did. It seems that they chose the latter.

I'm just an armchair opinion maker, but after all these GPU releases it seems that:
- Nvidia has reached a wall with increasing GPU performance with the way they did improving the 700-900-1000 series. Maybe they just ran out of ideas.
- They tried to build a moat around their existing GPU business and at the same time attack the competition by developing RT cores and working with game developers to make use of their RT cores, thus widening the performance gap with the AMD cards for future game releases.
- AMD has yet to have something viable to offer, to counter Nvidia's moves in this space. Don't know why, though I hope that they try to compete in this area. More competition is always better -- we have seen how market leaders become idle when there is no competititon. Intel from the Sandy Bridge era up to the Kaby Lake chips, and Nvidia from 1000 to 2000 series, although in this case they did improve performance a bit and add new technology, but they jacked up the prices so much because it was clear that there was to be no competition from AMD, or Intel for that matter, at least for the short term.

Nothing wrong with that, except that this is very similar to AMD's attempt in 2011 to create a multicore ecosystem on the desktop. At the time, apps and games weren't optimized for multithreaded use / multicore CPU's. However, as time went on we see how the multicore approach can yield better performance even in gaming, where previously only the single core performance seems to matter the most. I predict that Nvidia's RTX cards will become even more relevant in the coming years, as more and more games get optimized for real-time ray tracing and make the best use of RTX cards' RT cores. The difference between AMD's move in 2011 and Nvidia's move in 2018 is one of a market position -- in 2011, AMD was still the underdog, while in 2018 Nvidia had the upper hand.

Let's see what AMD will bring to the competition in 2019!

author: @olav947

text:
Steve, Tim, I've bin watching every video you have bin uploading ever since I found your channel back at 2016 xD

Back then I was getting back into computer hardware after about 8 years of absence I was desperate to find out what I missed out, what was happening out in the world while I was gone from the Silicon show. Turned out that I had A LOT to learn... So I started learning... But to learn I needed trustworthy sources... Took me more than 5 months before I finally found my trustworthy sources which I will put in a list without any preference of the order: @Hardware Unboxed; @Gamers Nexus; @Linus Tech Tips; @JayzTwoCents; @Science Studio; @Paul's Hardware; @OC3D; @AdoredTV. I sourced all of you by random, clicking on "recommended" videos by youtube and actually listening what you were saying, figuring out the way each of you work, the way you test, the way you make your date visible, the manner you use to get results. I got a degree in Physics, so I knew how to analyze data the right way, so I was listening to each one of you, how you collected the data and how you analyzed it. After getting a positive result for what I was searching I said to myself "Okay, these guys I trust, these guys I will recommend to my friends if they want to learn for themselves, these guys I will reference if I get asked on a piece of hardware". 
For me it was a long journey... Imagine missing out on all the tech from the Sandy Bridge era to present day :D
At the present day all of my coworkers look up to me for advice on their PCs or laptops (hardware ain't my only trick), so I have to answer to at least 50-60 questions a week from co-workers(we're "just" 300 people in this work place alone, I don't want to imagine what will happen if we get consolidated the whole 11 factories into one big building...). 
When the 2060 reviews went out, I started getting questions about it "Hey, you heard about it? Do you like it? What do you think about it?" but at that time I was only saying "So far I don't got all my data, I have only a partial picture, hold on, don't rush before knowing most of what's there to know". Ofc I've watched the videos from the mentioned above people, ofc I trust them, but that was not the FULL PICTURE! You guys were silent! And I was wondering: "Hey they didn't put out a video, what's up with that? I cant tell my friends or coworkers my full opinion on the card because I didn't see your video on it...
Keep up the good work guys! If not for something else, for the guys that are in a very bad place of the woods, where tech is more overpriced than even down under in Aussie land xD
@Good Old Gamer! So nice to see you commenting here too :D Okay, it seems everything did a full circle (for me at least). You are one of my newest YT subscriptions and I do like your content too xD

I'm sorry if the comment is too big or maybe too off topic, but for me you guys are valuable and I rly hate it that you got left out of the loop, probably because you were honest to the bone!
No matter what will happen I will continue watching every single video you put out from 1st to last minute :D

Unfortunately it make sense that this is the price of honest review content. If you're a company who makes things, you want the hype to be positive to maximize sales. That just works, expecting them to take a loss making and shipping a product to someone who might hurt their sales is poor value. You can't really expect (and many of you will anyway) a company to not work in their own best interest and distribute cards across a balanced review field. This is important, because this is the fundamental reason people need to stop pre-ordering things. People who get preview copies of things, are people the company are pretty sure will give them a good review. If when RTX is enabled framerates are cut in half this technology is then necessary for future sales and development of new architectures.

text:
I like your reviews and it sucks that you didn't have day 1 coverage. Having said that, I don't agree with your insinuation that it's because you are doing honest reviews or the implication that others aren't. The RTX series was heavily panned by almost everyone, most of whom got the 2060. Gamers Nexus tore these cards a new asshole and not only did they get the 2060 but also the Titan RTX. It's one thing to throw shade at NVIDIA but it's not fair to other publications to say that they only get review samples because they are not being honest enough. 

Also, there's a difference between being honest and beating a horse into the ground and then continue beating it. After a point your RTX coverage just seemed like you ragging on the product, with hyper focus on the negatives and no mention of any of the positive features that RTX has or will enable in the future. Sure, hardware isn't tested based on future promises but these features are coming, we all know they are, and anyone who bought these cards will be able to use them. A real honest review would have covered both the positive and negative aspects instead of just having a consistently negative tone because that's what the people wanted to see. I'm sure it's fun to have the commenters cheer you on as you make yet another video bashing NVIDIA or RTX but these people won't be sending you review units for your day one coverage. Being truthful to your audience is important but not at the expense of damaging your relationship with companies to a point where they start avoiding you. 

I don't personally think that's why NVIDIA didn't sample you guys early. If that were the case, there would be several other channels they'd have blacklisted. Considering the 2060 got universal praise, they wouldn't have been worried about the negative coverage from anyone. It may actually just be a mistake. But either way, maybe it's time to reassess a few things, about what is and isn't "honest" coverage and perhaps not throwing other media outlets under the bus while proving your high ground.

text:
It seems to me that nVidia are a bit touchy when it comes to accepting honesty. Seeing the other reviews, I can imagine what you would say about value for money and what, to a growing number of consumers, seems to be a fleecing of the fan base. There are many (and this has been the argument of "Not an apple fan") who, given 2 cards of the same price, the faster one by AMD and the lesser by nVidia, will still buy the nVidia product regardless. We have the situation now where, with the up to date drivers, the RX580 seems much better value these days than the nVidia 1060 -- and yet there is a certain YouTube channel doing monthly builds at 3 price points that still recommends the 1060 over the 580. I bet they got the 2060 sample!! We have the 590 that is most cases beats the 1060 even more than the 580 and can be had about the same price or slightly less (at least in UK) and yet all versions of the 1060 ships way more. 
Well, I think AMD don't need to rush. Their products are already better value. Maybe not as many bells and whistles, but they are at least not screwing their fan base. 
Another guaranteed of another sample is a channel I have had a lot of respect for in the past. That being Tech of Tomorrow. He came to the conclusions that the 2060 is "a great budget card"! What??? Since when was £350 budget??? (Pound price seems to compare to dollar price, despite the exchange rate showing that it should cost fewer pounds than dollars.... I heard that there was an Australia tax on prices, well it seems we have the same in UK.) To many I speak to, budget cards max at around £150, maybe up to £180. Anything more than that is mid range, and that tier ends at about £300 - no matter what the marketing or attempted price jigging of card manufacturers. The best that can be said about price range is that the 2060 is an OK upper mid range (accepting that the mid range of most of the builders I know would stretch the point another £50...)
So.... what it seems to me is that we have a card with the numbering scheme of the 1060, performance of the 1070, and at the price point of the 1070 with the bonus being the RTX bolt on.
Next generation, for most consumers, actually means better performance at the same price point paid at the previous generation. What nVidia are doing is trying to kid us that the successor to the 1060 is so much better that it deserves a £100 minimum top up in price. What we actually have is a rejigging of the model numbers to give this impression, and that it is just a load of garbage and BS. We actually have the 1070 range equivalent with a tiny boost in performance over the previous generation. And if anything is like the other RTX cards, when you can actually buy them from suppliers, it will be way more than the previous generation in price.
I am not fooled. This is not even mid range. It is like the 1070, which most builders treated already as though it was entering the luxury price area.  
So the next release will continue this act of smoke and mirrors. The next will be the actual replacement for the 1060, but will be called the 2050. It will have barely any performance increase over the previous generation, probably no RTX facility, but hey - it's miles better than even the 1050ti and so deserves the £100 hike in price. But it will not be the replacement for the 1050 - it's actually the replacement for the 1060 and hardly worth the wait in actuality. The replacement for the 1050 will be the 2030 or some such.
This is smoke and mirrors and marketing garbage. I am not fooled. And I am not going to allow myself to be ripped off.
I have seen many disgruntled people on many forums, and this marketing BS is nVidia turning a corner with their fan base. They just need to continue with this utter garbage to drive their fans to AMD or even, in future, to Intel.
After NPP, what they have done to you guys with the samples is not a surprise to me at all. Nvidia have revealed themselves to be the unscrupulous cowboy company that they really are.

text:
This is exactly the sort of thing that gives Nvidia their bad name. They can flex their muscles now, but once they’ve got some more competition they’ll have to be a bit more flexible. This situation reminds me of what’s happened in automotive journalism over the last decade. “Influencers” are being lent cars by premium brands more than journalists because they always give positive coverage. In some instances, Ferrari has blacklisted journalists and just refused to let them review anything in their product range due to negative coverage. In one example, Ferrari lost out in the Evo magazine car of the years to Porsche and actually called the magazine to express their anger over a subjective opinion, threatening to not lend them cars in future.

Intel aren’t stupid and will not be entering this market with something bad. Hopefully AMD will put some Ryzen success money into their GPU R&D and become more competitive too. Nvidia won’t get to behave like this for long and well done for remaining independent in the face of such bullshit.

text:
Imagine that, a huge tech company doesn't like when reviews are honest.

Personally I can't thank you enough for the info you've provided over the years. Always spot on without Bias or simply saying what Companies/People want to hear and compromising your ability to give open, honest reviews. You've done this even if it meant hurting your channel as we are seeing now. NVidia has for the last decade basically brought minimum upgrades from previous gens and they always hold something back to tip the market when needed, even if they have to gimp their own product to facilitate it. There's also the whole driver debacle where it can be argued they handicapped their older gen cards simply to sell a next generation. Their Tier/Performance/Pricing has almost never kept the end users best interest in mind. It's about profit above all else even if it means taking advantage of their customers. Don't get me wrong I'm no Fan Boy for AMD either but at least they put their cards on the table and release at launch a full line with clear Price/Performance/Tiers. I can think of but one instance, limiting the VRMs of the Vega 56 even though they can handle much more than they allow them to with factory. The whole China 570 as a 580 was also a definite black eye. Generally though with them at least you know exactly what your getting and don't have to worry that six months down the road they'll unlock the full potential of a card you've bought that they deliberately gimped to create false Tier/Performance/Pricing. We do from time to time see re-launches or refreshes of older products but they normally are accompanied by a release explaining why it's been done. For myself the refinement of of their product giving better performance for the same price isn't a negative...

Sorry for the TLDR:
You keep doing your honest reviews as you've always done and I'll keep watching...
As for NVidia deciding they didn't need your opinion it just proves exactly what I've said above. They've never had the best interest of gamer's at heart, it's always been about all profit all the time. I mean who builds and designs a product then proceeds to handicap said product to varying degrees to create rungs on the performance ladder that quite honestly don't need to exist. I'm sorry they've done this to you but the good things is you do have the ability to still do the reviews and there's now absolutely now doubt about your honesty...

text: @jscb7003  It really doesn't.  But it's really just the law of diminishing returns in reverse that it seems that way.  Since price increases for performance increases are nonlinear, it stands to reason that even if you increase the price of everything by a set linear percentage the effect will remain nonlinear.  So at the bottom of the stack, it will SEEM to be less nonsensical.  In reality you're still spending the same percentage more for much much less.  As revealed in GN's teardown, this is the x06 cut-down version.  The 2070 is the x06 full version.  By all normal past convention, the 2070 should have been the 2060 and the 2060 a cut-down 2060.  Perspective.

The same mfg uses gimmicks like "cage free" and "organic" to market two brands of eggs for significantly more than market price.  These gimmicks really do offer some marginal benefits to the real nutritional content of the eggs, though, so there's a real reason to want to buy those eggs. author: @abigailpatridge2948

text:
@abigailpatridge2948  Riiight, but you're getting very caught up in the name. What matters in the end of the day, above everything else, is price & performance. The 2060 is the direct successor to the 1070 and 1070ti. Put the naming aside, they're in the same price brackets, so that's the competition (along with a Vega 56). Bottom line is that the 2060 offers slightly better performance than the 1070ti for less money... so it's straight up better value. There's not much it in (with price or performance), so it's hardly an exciting new product, but objectively it is slightly better value than the 1070/1070ti it replaces. 

Whereas many reviewers continued to recommend the 1080 and particularly the 1080ti after the 2070 and 2080 launched, I can't see any reason to buy a 1070 or 1070ti at current pricing if (and this is an "if") 2060s are available at MSRP. Of course, the lower tier 1060, as well as the RX 570 and 580 might offer better fps per dollar and so are technically better "value",  they're also significantly slower, so many consumers will justify spending more for the better performance (just like they have for last two years for a GTX 1070 or better). 

RE naming: FWIW I think it's pretty clear that Nvidia is trying to shift the consumer expectations around price with Turing much like Apple did with the iPhone X. Nvidia want consumers to think of $350 as the new "midrange". I personally don't like this move, but I also don't think I have the right to tell Nvidia what they can call their products at launch. The only time it's genuinely anti-consumer and should be called out is when a lower performing product is released that is potentially difficult to distinguish from an existing and higher performing part (e.g. 1060 3GB, 1030 DDR4, RX 580 2048SP). 


TL:DR, objectively speaking, the 2060 is slightly better value than the 1070 and 1070ti it replaces, so at least it has a place in the market.

text:
See, this is why I & many others do and will continue to watch/read your content Steve. Bc you keep your integrity as opposed to "selling out" or becoming shills for one or both companies. And this will pay off in the long run. Like you said, you're working for us, on our side, not them or on theirs. And it is us that help keep you afloat and put food on the table. Sure, there's 2 sides to this equation, in that they are the ones that provide you the actual product to review. But without us, there would be no reason or purpose for any of your work whatsoever. You might as well try to sell forks to dogs. One of us can be "replaced" (them) while the other absolutely can't (us). 

You are a consumer advocate, not a member of their marketing arm. They don't directly pay you a salary in order to have you do exactly what Mr. Boss tells you to. Well neither do we, but like I said, it's bc of us you're doing what you do in the first place, not them. No us, no job. We are your end customers, your market (along with ad companies I'm sure. But same goes for them as well. No us, no readership/viewership, no ads), while they are not your employer. Keep doing what you do the way you have and we'll continue to support you so you can bypass them and continue to produce the great content & data that you have been. We can replace them and actually become both sides of the equation, supporting you both directly & indirectly. And keeping your integrity + providing honest, unbiased reviews will go a long way. More integrity means more respect from the community. More respect means more trust. More trust means overall more growth, more reach, more power, and your words having a greater impact and value as a whole. Making you an indispensable voice. Soon the tables might even actually turn and they become the ones trembling at your feet, afraid to get on your bad side, for fear of your influence. Trust me, you do not want to go too far in the opposite direction. Look at Tom's HW and where that has got them. Throwing their respect completely out the window and just being a laughing stock of a meme of a joke of a site. Their words & views are utterly meaningless to anyone besides fanboys and/or those who are serious about this industry/hobby. They hold absolutely no weight nor value. This is where shilling takes you. You start to suck up to these companies as a way get ahead or stay in the game, but in the end you start relying on them too much as to lose your independence. Becoming so dependent on them you essentially just end up being under their wing, w/ them basically owning you. Which I'm sure they'd love. Cheapest acquisition in history. Paid purely in early review sample video cards lol. And ppl will catch on sooner or later. Once that goes, the first thing to go w/ it is your reputation. Which is everything in journalism/the press.

Anyways just know you've got your supporters bc of exactly how you carry out your business. Keep your head up and don't change, it's all for the best in the long run. As an added bonus, you might actually sleep better at night too lol. It's a shame Nvidia don't think you're propaganda enough for them. But not really. More like an honor in my book.
